items.title: The Art of Loop Engineering: How to Build Agents That Improve Over Time
items.description:

Production-ready agents need the right loops around them: loops that help them complete tasks, verify their work, respond to real-world events, and improve over time.

Hear from Sydney Runkle at LangChain, for a practical session on loop engineering, the emerging design pattern behind reliable agent systems. 

You'll learn how these loops fit together, where human oversight matters most, and how teams can use our open source frameworks and LangSmith, our platform for agent engineering, to build agents that are not only capable, but observable, testable, and continuously improving.

items.title: Build a secure computer for your agent
items.description:
Most agents today aren't just calling APIs. They're writing and running code, processing files, browsing the web, iterating across multi-step tasks. That means they need more than tools, they need a real workspace: a file system, a shell, installed packages, and state that persists across steps.

But the moment you give an agent execution access, you've introduced a new category of production problem. Model-generated code is untrusted. Local execution doesn't scale. And vanilla containers fall short when you actually need isolation, credential safety, cost controls, and the ability to reproduce what an agent did three sessions ago.

In this session, Amy and Mukil walk through how to give agents their own computer without giving up control:
- The architecture patterns behind production-ready sandboxed execution and when to build your own vs. use a managed sandbox
- What "production-ready" actually requires: secure execution, credential management, resource limits, fast provisioning, snapshots, forks, and persistent state
- How coding agents, data analysis agents, and file-processing workflows behave differently in isolated environments, and what becomes possible when infrastructure stops being the bottleneck

items.title: the PERFECT Raspberry Pi wall dashboard?
items.description:
This video is sponsored by NetworkChuck Coffee. Grab a bag of Default Route (my favorite) and fuel your next build: https://ntck.co/coffee

Raspberry Pi sent me the new Raspberry Pi Touch Display 2, the 10 inch portrait version, and I mounted it on my studio wall to run all my Home Assistant and homelab stuff. It is a gorgeous little screen (1200x1920, real IPS, 10 finger touch, 400 nits) and at $80 it is a steal. There is one catch though, and a lot of you are not going to like it: this thing only works on the Raspberry Pi 5 and the Compute Modules. Your Pi 3 or Pi 4 will not work at all.

In this video I unbox it, walk through everything that is new versus the old touch display, hit a wall when it powered on and did absolutely nothing (turns out you have to update the firmware on your Pi 5, the EEPROM, before it will recognize the screen), mount it with nothing but a drill and some screws, and finally turn it into a beautiful Home Assistant dashboard using an open source kiosk app called TouchKio. Whether you are building a smart home wall panel, a homelab status board, or you just want your Raspberry Pi to show off what it is doing, this is a really good option.

items.title: FDE - This new job title is showing up everywhere
items.description:
A new job title is showing up everywhere in tech hiring right now.
Forward Deployed Engineer.

Most people read it and assume it is a fancy name for a software engineer who travels.

That misses the point completely.

A regular engineer receives a requirement document, builds what it says, and ships it.

An FDE does not get that comfort.

They sit at the client's location. The client explains the problem in their own words. Sometimes the client changes their mind halfway through the conversation.

The FDE has to understand the business context, decide what should actually be built, and build it right there using AI tools.

Same problem, ten different clients, ten different solutions.

That is why this role sits at an unusual intersection.

Engineer + product manager + consultant.

Coding is only one third of the job. The other two thirds are listening carefully, asking better questions, and turning messy business language into something buildable.

Which is exactly why many strong coders struggle here, and why people with communication skills suddenly become very valuable.

For anyone preparing for this path, technical skill is the entry ticket. Communication and product thinking decide the outcome.

The full breakdown is in the video, including a simple analogy that explains the role in thirty seconds.

What matters more in a role like this, deep technical depth or client communication? #short

items.title: RAG Explained The Most In Demand Pattern in AI Engineering
items.description:
RAG, or retrieval augmented generation, is probably the most in-demand pattern in AI engineering right now. It's been around a few years and it's still wildly popular, and a huge percentage of the real AI apps you use have some form of it.

The concept is simple: the model was trained on general data, but your user wants answers about their data, and RAG closes that gap. You take that data and store it in something like a vector database. Then when someone asks a question, you search the database, find the most relevant results, and feed them into the model so it can reason over them. 

Now the model has both its original training data and the specific context from your user. It's one of the most useful things large language models can do, and it's harder than it looks once you're doing it at scale.

events.title: The Art of Loop Engineering: How to Build Agents That Improve Over Time

viewpoints.summary:
Agents are useful because they can take action, but getting them to do valuable work reliably takes more than giving a model access to tools. Production-ready agents need the right loops around them: loops that help them complete tasks, verify their work, respond to real-world events, and improve over time.

Hear from Sydney Runkle at LangChain, for a practical session on loop engineering, the emerging design pattern behind reliable agent systems. 

You'll learn how these loops fit together, where human oversight matters most, and how teams can use our open source frameworks and LangSmith, our platform for agent engineering, to build agents that are not only capable, but observable, testable, and continuously improving.

Most agents today aren't just calling APIs. They're writing and running code, processing files, browsing the web, iterating across multi-step tasks. That means they need more than tools, they need a real workspace: a file system, a shell, installed packages, and state that persists across steps.

But the moment you give an agent execution access, you've introduced a new category of production problem. Model-generated code is untrusted. Local execution doesn't scale. And vanilla containers fall short when you actually need isolation, credential safety, cost controls, and the ability to reproduce what an agent did three sessions ago.

In this session, Amy and Mukil walk through how to give agents their own computer without giving up control:
- The architecture patterns behind production-ready sandboxed execution and when to build your own vs. use a managed sandbox
- What "production-ready" actually requires: secure execution, credential management, resource limits, fast provisioning, snapshots, forks, and persistent state
- How coding agents, data analysis agents, and file-processing workflows behave differently in isolated environments, and what becomes possible when infrastructure stops being the bottleneck

events.title: FDE - This new job title is showing up everywhere

viewpoints.summary:
A new job title is showing up everywhere in tech hiring right now.
Forward Deployed Engineer.

Most people read it and assume it is a fancy name for a software engineer who travels.

That misses the point completely.

A regular engineer receives a requirement document, builds what it says, and ships it.

An FDE does not get that comfort.

They sit at the client's location. The client explains the problem in their own words. Sometimes the client changes their mind halfway through the conversation.

The FDE has to understand the business context, decide what should actually be built, and build it right there using AI tools.

Same problem, ten different clients, ten different solutions.

That is why this role sits at an unusual intersection.

Engineer + product manager + consultant.

Coding is only one third of the job. The other two thirds are listening carefully, asking better questions, and turning messy business language into something buildable.

Which is exactly why many strong coders struggle here, and why people with communication skills suddenly become very valuable.

For anyone preparing for this path, technical skill is the entry ticket. Communication and product thinking decide the outcome.

The full breakdown is in the video, including a simple analogy that explains the role in thirty seconds.

What matters more in a role like this, deep technical depth or client communication? #short

events.title: RAG Explained The Most In Demand Pattern in AI Engineering

viewpoints.summary:
RAG, or retrieval augmented generation, is probably the most in-demand pattern in AI engineering right now. It's been around a few years and it's still wildly popular, and a huge percentage of the real AI apps you use have some form of it.

The concept is simple: the model was trained on general data, but your user wants answers about their data, and RAG closes that gap. You take that data and store it in something like a vector database. Then when someone asks a question, you search the database, find the most relevant results, and feed them into the model so it can reason over them. 

Now the model has both its original training data and the specific context from your user. It's one of the most useful things large language models can do, and it's harder than it looks once you're doing it at scale.
